questions.stem: A hoop, a solid disk, and a solid sphere are released from rest at the top of the ramp shown and roll without slipping. The objects have different masses and radii. Which of the following correctly predicts the order in which they reach the bottom?
choices: Sphere, then disk, then hoop, regardless of their masses and radii
Hoop, then disk, then sphere, regardless of their masses and radii
The object with the smallest mass arrives first.
They arrive together, because all objects fall with the same acceleration.
questions.explanation: For rolling without slipping, the acceleration depends only on how the mass is distributed, through the factor \(\dfrac{I}{MR^2}\): \(\tfrac{2}{5}\) for the sphere, \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) for the disk, and \(1\) for the hoop. The smaller that fraction, the smaller the share of energy that goes into rotation and the faster the object travels.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping along a horizontal floor and then moves up a ramp. In trial 1 the ramp is rough enough that the ball rolls without slipping. In trial 2 the ramp is frictionless. How do the maximum heights the ball reaches compare?
choices: It rises higher in trial 2, because no energy is dissipated by friction.
The heights are equal, because the ball has the same total kinetic energy at the bottom.
It rises higher in trial 1, because its rotational kinetic energy is also converted to potential energy.
It rises higher in trial 2, because friction opposes the motion in trial 1.
questions.explanation: On the frictionless ramp nothing exerts a torque on the ball, so it keeps spinning at the same rate and only its translational kinetic energy becomes potential energy. On the rough ramp static friction, which dissipates no energy, slows the rotation, so all of the kinetic energy is converted.

questions.stem: A skater spinning on frictionless ice pulls her arms in, reducing her rotational inertia to one third of its original value. By what factor does her rotational kinetic energy change?
choices: It increases by a factor of 9.
It decreases by a factor of 3.
It increases by a factor of 3.
questions.explanation: Angular momentum \(I\omega\) is conserved, so her angular speed triples. Rotational kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2=\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\), so reducing \(I\) to one third triples the energy. The skater does work in pulling her arms inward.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) spins freely with angular speed \(\omega_0\) about a vertical axle through its center. A thin ring of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), initially not rotating, is dropped onto the disk so that their centers coincide, and friction brings them to a common angular speed. The rotational inertia of the disk is \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\) and that of the ring is \(MR^2\). What is the final angular speed?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\omega_0=\left(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2+MR^2\right)\omega\), so \(\omega=\dfrac{\omega_0}{3}\). Assuming kinetic energy is conserved instead gives \(\dfrac{\omega_0}{\sqrt{3}}\), but the friction between the surfaces dissipates energy.

questions.stem: A child stands at the rim of a merry-go-round that rotates freely on a frictionless axle. The child walks to the center. For the system of the child and the merry-go-round, which of the following describes the changes in angular momentum and rotational kinetic energy?
choices: The angular momentum and the kinetic energy both stay the same.
The angular momentum stays the same and the kinetic energy increases.
The angular momentum increases and the kinetic energy stays the same.
The angular momentum stays the same and the kinetic energy decreases.
questions.explanation: No external torque acts, so the angular momentum is constant. The rotational inertia decreases, so the angular speed increases, and the kinetic energy \(\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\) increases. The additional energy comes from the work the child does in walking inward.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in an elliptical orbit around a planet. Its speed is \(v\) at its closest point, a distance \(r\) from the planet's center. What is its speed at its farthest point, a distance \(4r\) from the planet's center?
questions.explanation: The gravitational force points toward the planet and exerts no torque about it, so the satellite's angular momentum is conserved. At the closest and farthest points the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so \(mvr=mv'(4r)\) and \(v'=\dfrac{v}{4}\).

questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) lies at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface and can rotate about a fixed pivot at one end. A lump of clay of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) perpendicular to the rod strikes the free end and sticks, as shown. The rotational inertia of the rod about the pivot is \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\). What is the angular speed of the rod just after the collision?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum about the pivot is conserved: \(mvL=\left(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2+mL^2\right)\omega\). Solving gives \(\omega=\dfrac{3mv}{(M+3m)L}\).

questions.stem: A lump of clay strikes and sticks to the free end of a rod that can rotate about a fixed pivot at its other end, as shown. For the system of the clay and the rod, which quantities are conserved during the collision?
choices: Angular momentum about the pivot only
Linear momentum and angular momentum about the pivot
Linear momentum, angular momentum about the pivot, and kinetic energy
questions.explanation: The pivot exerts an external force on the rod during the collision, so linear momentum is not conserved. That force acts at the pivot, so it exerts no torque about the pivot and angular momentum about that point is conserved. Kinetic energy is dissipated because the clay sticks.

questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere, with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), rolls without slipping along a horizontal surface. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?
questions.explanation: With \(\omega=\dfrac{v}{R}\), the rotational kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\right)\dfrac{v^2}{R^2}=\tfrac{1}{5}Mv^2\) and the translational kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2\). The rotational fraction is \(\dfrac{1/5}{7/10}=\dfrac{2}{7}\).

questions.stem: A flywheel with rotational inertia \(3.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) starts from rest and is acted on by a constant net torque of \(6.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) as it turns through \(25\text{ rad}\). What is its final angular speed?
questions.explanation: The work done by the torque is \(\tau\,\Delta\theta=150\text{ J}\). Setting this equal to \(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\) gives \(\omega^2=100\), so \(\omega=10\text{ rad/s}\).

questions.stem: A wheel is initially at rest on a frictionless axle. A net torque of \(4.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) acts on it for \(3.0\text{ s}\), followed immediately by a net torque of \(2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) in the opposite direction for \(2.0\text{ s}\). What is the magnitude of the wheel's angular momentum at the end of the \(5.0\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The change in angular momentum equals the angular impulse, the net torque multiplied by the time it acts: \(4.0(3.0)-2.0(2.0)=8.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{/s}\). The rotational inertia is not needed.

questions.stem: A solid sphere and a hoop of equal mass are released from rest at the top of the ramp shown and roll without slipping. How do their kinetic energies compare at the bottom?
choices: Their total kinetic energies are equal, and so are their translational kinetic energies.
The sphere has more total kinetic energy, because it is moving faster.
The hoop has more total kinetic energy, because it has more rotational inertia.
Their total kinetic energies are equal, and the sphere has more translational kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Each object converts the same potential energy \(mgh\) into kinetic energy, so the totals are equal. The hoop puts half of its kinetic energy into rotation and the sphere only two sevenths, so the sphere has more translational kinetic energy and reaches the bottom moving faster.

questions.stem: A comet moves around the Sun in a highly elongated elliptical orbit. Where in its orbit is the comet moving fastest, and why?
choices: At its closest point to the Sun, because its angular momentum about the Sun is constant and its distance is smallest there.
At its farthest point from the Sun, because the gravitational force on it is weakest there.
At its closest point to the Sun, because the Sun exerts a torque that speeds it up there.
Its speed is the same everywhere, because the mechanical energy of the comet–Sun system is constant.
questions.explanation: The gravitational force points along the line to the Sun, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and the comet's angular momentum is conserved. A smaller distance therefore requires a greater speed. Equivalently, the system's potential energy is lowest at the closest point, so the kinetic energy is highest.

questions.stem: A student sits at rest on a stool that can rotate freely about a vertical axis. The student holds a wheel with its axle vertical; the wheel is spinning counterclockwise as seen from above. The student turns the wheel over so that it spins clockwise as seen from above. What happens to the student and the stool?
choices: They rotate clockwise, with an angular momentum equal to the wheel's original angular momentum.
They rotate counterclockwise, with an angular momentum equal to the wheel's original angular momentum.
They rotate counterclockwise, with an angular momentum equal to twice the wheel's original angular momentum.
They remain at rest, because the wheel's angular speed has not changed.
questions.explanation: No external torque acts about the vertical axis, so the total angular momentum stays equal to the wheel's original value \(L\), counterclockwise. After the flip the wheel has \(-L\), so the student and stool must have \(+2L\) for the total to remain \(L\).

questions.stem: A lump of clay strikes the free end of a pivoted rod and sticks, as shown, giving the rod an angular speed \(\omega\). The experiment is repeated with a rubber ball of the same mass and speed, which bounces straight back. How does the rod's angular speed just after the collision compare with \(\omega\)?
choices: It is smaller, because the ball does not stay with the rod.
It is the same, because the ball and the clay have the same angular momentum before the collision.
It is smaller, because the ball keeps some kinetic energy.
It is greater, because the ball's angular momentum about the pivot changes by a larger amount.
questions.explanation: The total angular momentum about the pivot is conserved. The clay ends up with a small angular momentum in its original direction, while the ball's angular momentum reverses direction, so the ball's change is larger and the rod receives more angular momentum.

questions.stem: A bowling ball is released onto a rough horizontal lane sliding at speed \(v\) without rotating. Which of the following describes its motion afterward?
choices: Its speed and its rate of rotation both decrease until it stops.
Its speed stays constant while its rate of rotation increases.
Its speed decreases and its rate of rotation increases until it rolls without slipping, and then both remain constant.
Its speed decreases until it stops, and then it begins to roll.
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction acts backward at the point of contact, which slows the ball's center and also exerts a torque that spins the ball up. Once the speed of the center equals \(R\omega\), the contact point no longer slides, the kinetic friction disappears, and the ball rolls at constant speed.

questions.stem: A uniform solid cylinder, with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\), rolls without slipping at \(4.0\text{ m/s}\) along level ground and then rolls up a ramp. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), how high does its center rise?
questions.explanation: Rolling without slipping, the cylinder's kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2+\tfrac{1}{4}Mv^2=\tfrac{3}{4}Mv^2=12M\). Setting this equal to \(Mgh\) gives \(h=1.2\text{ m}\). A sliding block would rise \(0.80\text{ m}\), a hoop \(1.6\text{ m}\), and a sphere \(1.12\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: A disk with rotational inertia \(2.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) spins at \(3.0\text{ rad/s}\) on a frictionless axle. A second disk with rotational inertia \(1.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\), not spinning, is dropped onto it along the same axle, and they reach a common angular speed. How much kinetic energy is dissipated?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: \(2.0(3.0)=3.0\omega\), so \(\omega=2.0\text{ rad/s}\). The kinetic energy falls from \(\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(3.0)^2=9.0\text{ J}\) to \(\tfrac{1}{2}(3.0)(2.0)^2=6.0\text{ J}\). Friction between the disks dissipates the difference.

questions.stem: The string wrapped around the uniform disk shown supports a block of mass \(m\). The disk has mass \(M\), radius \(R\), and rotational inertia \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\), and turns on a frictionless axle. The block is released from rest. What is its speed after it has fallen a distance \(h\)?
questions.explanation: The lost potential energy \(mgh\) becomes the block's kinetic energy and the disk's: \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\dfrac{v^2}{R^2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(m+\tfrac{1}{2}M\right)v^2\). Solving for \(v\) gives the result. The disk behaves like an extra mass of \(\tfrac{1}{2}M\).

questions.stem: A \(2.0\text{ kg}\) puck slides at \(3.0\text{ m/s}\) in a straight line that passes \(4.0\text{ m}\) from point P. What is the magnitude of the puck's angular momentum about P?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum about a point is \(mvd\), where \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of motion: \(2.0(3.0)(4.0)=24\). An object moving in a straight line has angular momentum about any point not on that line.

questions.stem: Two identical disks spin on frictionless axles, and disk 1 spins twice as fast as disk 2. How do their angular momenta and rotational kinetic energies compare?
choices: Disk 1 has twice the angular momentum and twice the kinetic energy.
Disk 1 has four times the angular momentum and four times the kinetic energy.
They have the same angular momentum, and disk 1 has twice the kinetic energy.
Disk 1 has twice the angular momentum and four times the kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: With the same rotational inertia, angular momentum \(I\omega\) is proportional to \(\omega\), while kinetic energy \(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\) is proportional to \(\omega^2\).

questions.stem: A wheel rolls without slipping along level ground, and its center moves at speed \(v\). What are the speeds, relative to the ground, of the point at the top of the wheel and the point touching the ground?
choices: \(2v\) at the top and \(0\) at the bottom
\(v\) at the top and \(v\) at the bottom, in opposite directions
\(0\) at the top and \(2v\) at the bottom
questions.explanation: Each point's velocity is the center's velocity \(v\) plus its velocity due to rotation, \(R\omega=v\). At the top the two add; at the contact point they cancel, which is what "without slipping" means.

questions.stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping down a ramp, and a block slides down an identical, frictionless ramp. Both start from rest at the same height. Which reaches the bottom first?
choices: The cylinder, because rolling involves less friction
The block, because none of its energy goes into rotation
They arrive together, because they descend the same height
The cylinder, because it gains rotational kinetic energy as well
questions.explanation: Both convert the same fraction of their mass's potential energy per unit mass into kinetic energy, but the cylinder must share it between translation and rotation. At every height the block moves faster, so it arrives first.

questions.stem: A constant net torque acts on a wheel that starts from rest. Which describes a graph of the wheel's angular momentum as a function of time?
choices: A parabola, because the wheel's angle increases quadratically
A horizontal line, because the torque is constant
A curve that levels off at a maximum value
A straight line through the origin with a slope equal to the torque
questions.explanation: Net torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, \(\tau=\dfrac{\Delta L}{\Delta t}\). A constant torque changes the angular momentum at a constant rate.

figure.alt: Position versus time graph of an oscillator: a cosine curve with amplitude 0.2 m and period 2 s, starting at x = 0.2 m when t = 0

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block oscillating on a spring as a function of time. What is the maximum speed of the block?
questions.explanation: The amplitude is \(A=0.20\text{ m}\) and the period is \(T=2.0\text{ s}\), so \(\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=\pi\text{ rad/s}\). The maximum speed is \(A\omega=0.20\pi\approx 0.63\text{ m/s}\). The average speed over a cycle is \(\dfrac{4A}{T}=0.40\text{ m/s}\).

figure.alt: Position versus time graph of an oscillator: a cosine curve with amplitude 0.2 m and period 2 s, starting at x = 0.2 m when t = 0

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block oscillating on a spring as a function of time. Which of the following describes the block's velocity and acceleration at \(t=0.5\text{ s}\)?
choices: The velocity is zero; the acceleration has its maximum magnitude and is negative.
The velocity and the acceleration are both zero.
The velocity has its maximum magnitude and is negative; the acceleration is zero.
The velocity has its maximum magnitude and is positive; the acceleration is zero.
questions.explanation: At \(t=0.5\text{ s}\) the block passes through equilibrium, where the graph is steepest and sloping downward, so the velocity is most negative. The restoring force, and therefore the acceleration, is zero at equilibrium.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) attached to a spring of spring constant \(k\) oscillates on a frictionless surface with period \(T\), as shown. The block is replaced with one of mass \(2m\), and the spring is replaced with one of spring constant \(\dfrac{k}{2}\). What is the new period?
questions.explanation: The period is \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\). Doubling the mass and halving the spring constant multiplies \(\dfrac{m}{k}\) by 4, so the period doubles.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates between \(x=-A\) and \(x=+A\) on a frictionless surface, as shown. The block is then set oscillating with amplitude \(2A\). How do the period, the maximum speed, and the total mechanical energy change?
choices: The period doubles, the maximum speed is unchanged, and the energy doubles.
The period is unchanged, the maximum speed doubles, and the energy doubles.
The period is unchanged, the maximum speed doubles, and the energy quadruples.
The period doubles, the maximum speed doubles, and the energy quadruples.
questions.explanation: The period of a spring–block oscillator depends only on mass and spring constant, not on amplitude. The total energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\), so it quadruples, and since that equals \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2\), the maximum speed doubles.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates between \(x=-A\) and \(x=+A\) on a frictionless surface, as shown, and its maximum speed is \(v_{\max}\). What is the speed of the block when it is at \(x=\dfrac{A}{2}\)?
questions.explanation: At \(x=\dfrac{A}{2}\) the potential energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}k\left(\tfrac{A}{2}\right)^2\), one fourth of the total, so the kinetic energy is three fourths of its maximum. Speed depends on the square root of kinetic energy, giving \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v_{\max}\).

questions.explanation: The period is \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\). Multiplying both the length and the field strength by 4 leaves \(\dfrac{L}{g}\) unchanged, so the period is the same.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum swings with a small amplitude, as shown. The bob is replaced with one of twice the mass, and the pendulum is released from twice the original angle, still a small angle. How does the period compare with the original period?
choices: It is longer by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).
questions.explanation: For small angles the period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length and the gravitational field strength. A greater mass increases the restoring force and the inertia in the same proportion, and a larger small amplitude means a greater distance covered at a proportionally greater speed.

questions.stem: When a block is hung from a vertical spring, the spring stretches a distance \(d\) before the block hangs at rest. The block is then pulled down slightly and released. What is the period of its oscillation?
choices: It cannot be determined without the mass of the block.
questions.explanation: At equilibrium \(kd=mg\), so \(\dfrac{m}{k}=\dfrac{d}{g}\). Substituting into \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\) gives \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{g}}\); the mass and spring constant are not needed separately.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) on a spring oscillates with amplitude \(A\) on a frictionless horizontal surface. At the instant the block passes through its equilibrium position, a lump of clay of mass \(m\) is dropped vertically onto the block and sticks. What is the amplitude of the oscillation afterward?
questions.explanation: Horizontal momentum is conserved as the clay lands, so the speed at equilibrium is halved while the mass doubles. The kinetic energy \(\tfrac{1}{2}(2m)\left(\tfrac{v}{2}\right)^2\) is half its previous value. Since the total energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\), halving the energy reduces the amplitude by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).

questions.stem: A \(0.50\text{ kg}\) block on a spring with spring constant \(200\text{ N/m}\) oscillates on a frictionless horizontal surface with amplitude \(0.10\text{ m}\). What is the speed of the block when it is \(0.060\text{ m}\) from equilibrium?
questions.explanation: The total energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(200)(0.10)^2=1.0\text{ J}\). At \(0.060\text{ m}\) the potential energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(200)(0.060)^2=0.36\text{ J}\), leaving \(0.64\text{ J}\) of kinetic energy, so \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.64)}{0.50}}=1.6\text{ m/s}\). The maximum speed is \(2.0\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: A simple pendulum and a block on a vertical spring both oscillate inside an elevator. The elevator begins to accelerate upward at a constant rate. How do the periods of the two oscillators change?
choices: The pendulum's period decreases and the spring–block period is unchanged.
The pendulum's period is unchanged and the spring–block period decreases.
questions.explanation: In the upward-accelerating elevator, objects behave as if the gravitational field strength were \(g+a\). The pendulum's period \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g+a}}\) decreases. The spring–block period \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\) does not depend on \(g\); only the equilibrium position shifts.

questions.stem: A block is attached to two identical springs. When the springs are connected side by side (in parallel), the block oscillates with period \(T_p\). When the springs are connected end to end (in series), it oscillates with period \(T_s\). What is \(\dfrac{T_s}{T_p}\)?
questions.explanation: In parallel the effective spring constant is \(2k\); in series it is \(\dfrac{k}{2}\). The period is proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}}}\), so \(\dfrac{T_s}{T_p}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2k}{k/2}}=2\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block oscillating on a spring as a function of time. At which of the following times is the kinetic energy of the block greatest?
questions.explanation: The block moves fastest as it passes through equilibrium, \(x=0\), where the graph is steepest; that happens at \(t=1.5\text{ s}\). At the other times listed the block is at maximum displacement, momentarily at rest, with all of the energy stored in the spring.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates between \(x=-A\) and \(x=+A\) on a frictionless surface, as shown. Which of the following is true at the instant the block is at \(x=+A\)?
choices: Its velocity and its acceleration are both zero.
Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration has its greatest magnitude and is directed away from \(x=0\).
Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration has its greatest magnitude and is directed toward \(x=0\).
Its velocity has its greatest magnitude and its acceleration is zero.
questions.explanation: At the turning point the block is momentarily at rest, but the spring is stretched the most, so the restoring force and the acceleration are greatest and point back toward equilibrium. If the acceleration were zero there, the block would stay at rest.

questions.stem: A block on a spring is released from rest at \(x=+A\), as shown. How does the time it takes to move from \(x=+A\) to \(x=\tfrac{A}{2}\) compare with the time it takes to move from \(x=\tfrac{A}{2}\) to \(x=0\)?
choices: The two intervals are equal, because the distances are equal.
The first interval is shorter, because the acceleration is greatest near the turning point.
The two intervals are equal, because the period does not depend on amplitude.
The first interval is longer, because the block is moving more slowly near the turning point.
questions.explanation: The block starts from rest at \(x=+A\) and is still slow as it reaches \(\tfrac{A}{2}\), while it covers the second half of the distance near its maximum speed. With \(x=A\cos\omega t\), the first interval lasts one sixth of a period and the second lasts one twelfth.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates with period \(T\). Which of the following describes how the kinetic energy of the block varies with time?
choices: It oscillates between zero and a maximum with period \(T\).
It oscillates between negative and positive values with period \(T\).
It oscillates between zero and a maximum with period \(\dfrac{T}{2}\).
It remains constant, because mechanical energy is conserved.
questions.explanation: The block passes through equilibrium, where its kinetic energy is greatest, twice in each cycle, once in each direction. Kinetic energy depends on the square of the velocity, so it is never negative and it repeats twice as often as the position does.

questions.stem: A \(0.50\text{ kg}\) block on a spring of spring constant \(200\text{ N/m}\) oscillates on a frictionless surface. What is its period?
questions.explanation: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.50}{200}}=2\pi(0.050)\approx 0.31\text{ s}\). Forgetting the factor \(2\pi\) gives \(0.050\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what length must a simple pendulum have so that its period is \(2.0\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: Solving \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\) for \(L\) gives \(L=\dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2}=\dfrac{10(4.0)}{39.5}\approx 1.0\text{ m}\). Period grows as the square root of length, so doubling the period would take four times the length.

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a \(0.50\text{ kg}\) block oscillating on a spring. What is the spring constant?
questions.explanation: The period is \(2.0\text{ s}\), so \(\omega=\pi\text{ rad/s}\). From \(\omega^2=\dfrac{k}{m}\), \(k=0.50\pi^2\approx 4.9\text{ N/m}\).

figure.alt: Position versus time graph of an oscillator: a cosine curve with amplitude 0.2 m and period 2 s, starting at x = 0.2 m when t = 0

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block on a spring with spring constant \(5.0\text{ N/m}\). What is the total mechanical energy of the oscillator?
questions.explanation: The amplitude is \(0.20\text{ m}\), and the total energy equals the spring energy at maximum displacement: \(\tfrac{1}{2}(5.0)(0.20)^2=0.10\text{ J}\).

questions.stem: A block on a horizontal spring oscillates on Earth with period \(T\). The same apparatus is taken to the Moon, where the gravitational field is about one sixth as strong. What is the period there?
questions.explanation: The period of a spring–block oscillator, \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\), depends only on the mass and the spring constant. Gravity does not provide the restoring force on a horizontal spring, unlike a pendulum.

questions.stem: A pendulum clock keeps correct time at room temperature. On a hot day its metal pendulum rod expands slightly. How does the clock behave?
choices: It runs fast, because a longer pendulum swings through a larger arc.
It runs slow, because a longer pendulum has a longer period.
It keeps correct time, because the period does not depend on length.
It runs fast, because the pendulum gains mass.
questions.explanation: The period of a pendulum is proportional to \(\sqrt{L}\). A longer rod takes longer for each swing, so the clock completes fewer ticks per hour and falls behind.

questions.skill: Velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion
questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates between \(x=-A\) and \(x=+A\). At an instant when it is at \(x=+\tfrac{A}{2}\) and moving toward equilibrium, which describes its velocity and acceleration?
choices: The velocity points in the \(-x\) direction and the acceleration in the \(+x\) direction, so the block is slowing down.
Both point in the \(-x\) direction, so the block is speeding up.
Both point in the \(+x\) direction, so the block is speeding up.
The velocity points in the \(-x\) direction and the acceleration is zero.
questions.explanation: The block moves toward equilibrium, in the \(-x\) direction. The restoring force always points toward equilibrium, also \(-x\) here. With velocity and acceleration in the same direction, the block speeds up until it reaches \(x=0\).

questions.stem: For a block oscillating on a spring, which describes a graph of the block's acceleration as a function of its position?
choices: A straight line through the origin with a positive slope
A horizontal line, because the spring constant is constant
A straight line through the origin with a negative slope
questions.explanation: Newton's second law with Hooke's law gives \(a=-\dfrac{k}{m}x\): the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it. This defining relationship of simple harmonic motion is linear in \(x\).

figure.alt: Position versus time graph of an oscillator: a cosine curve with amplitude 0.2 m and period 2 s, starting at x = 0.2 m when t = 0

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block oscillating on a spring. Which statement describes the block at \(t=1.0\text{ s}\)?
choices: Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration has its maximum value in the \(+x\) direction.
Its velocity is maximum, and its acceleration is zero.
Its velocity and its acceleration are both zero.
Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration has its maximum value in the \(-x\) direction.
questions.explanation: At \(t=1.0\text{ s}\) the block is at \(x=-0.20\text{ m}\), a turning point, so it is momentarily at rest. The stretched spring pulls it back toward equilibrium, in the \(+x\) direction, with the greatest force.

questions.stem: Water of density \(\rho\) flows through the horizontal pipe shown. The cross-sectional area at section 1 is four times the area at section 2, and the speed of the water at section 1 is \(v\). What is the pressure at section 1 minus the pressure at section 2?
questions.explanation: Continuity gives a speed of \(4v\) at section 2. Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe gives \(P_1-P_2=\tfrac{1}{2}\rho\left[(4v)^2-v^2\right]=\dfrac{15}{2}\rho v^2\). The pressure is higher where the water moves more slowly.

questions.stem: Water flows steadily from section 1 to section 2 of the horizontal pipe shown. Which of the following correctly explains how the pressure in the water changes?
choices: The pressure is higher at section 2, because the water is squeezed into a smaller space.
The pressure is the same at both sections, because the pipe is horizontal.
The pressure is higher at section 2, because the water there is moving faster and pushes harder on the walls.
The pressure is lower at section 2, because a net force toward section 2 is needed to speed the water up as it enters the narrow section.
questions.explanation: The water must speed up to pass through the narrow section at the same volume flow rate. An element of water entering the constriction accelerates forward, so the pressure behind it must be greater than the pressure ahead of it.

questions.stem: Water streams from a small hole in the side of a large open tank filled to height \(H\), as shown. At what depth \(h\) below the water surface should the hole be made so that the stream lands as far from the tank as possible?
choices: As close to the bottom of the tank as possible
As close to the water surface as possible
questions.explanation: The water leaves with speed \(\sqrt{2gh}\) and falls for a time \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2(H-h)}{g}}\), so it lands a distance \(2\sqrt{h(H-h)}\) away. That product is greatest when \(h=\dfrac{H}{2}\). A lower hole gives a faster stream but too little time to fall.

questions.stem: Water streams from a small hole in the side of a large open tank, as shown. The hole is \(0.80\text{ m}\) below the water surface. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what is the speed of the water as it leaves the hole?
questions.explanation: Applying Bernoulli's equation between the surface, where the water is nearly at rest, and the hole, both at atmospheric pressure, gives \(v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(10)(0.80)}=4.0\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: A block floats in water of density \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\) with three fourths of its volume submerged, as shown. The block is then placed in oil of density \(900\text{ kg/m}^3\). What fraction of the block's volume is submerged in the oil?
questions.explanation: A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid, so the submerged fraction equals the ratio of the object's density to the fluid's density. The block's density is \(750\text{ kg/m}^3\), so in oil the fraction is \(\dfrac{750}{900}=\dfrac{5}{6}\).

questions.stem: A boat carrying a heavy steel anchor floats in a small pond. The anchor is thrown overboard and sinks to the bottom. What happens to the water level of the pond?
choices: It rises, because the anchor now displaces water directly.
It stays the same, because the total mass in the pond has not changed.
It falls, because the sunken anchor displaces less water than it did while it was in the boat.
It rises, because the boat floats higher after the anchor is removed.
questions.explanation: While in the boat, the anchor causes the boat to displace a volume of water equal in weight to the anchor, which is much larger than the anchor's own volume because steel is denser than water. On the bottom it displaces only its own volume, so the total displaced volume decreases.

questions.stem: An object weighs \(30\text{ N}\) in air. When it is completely submerged in water of density \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\) and suspended from a spring scale, the scale reads \(20\text{ N}\). What is the density of the object?
questions.explanation: The buoyant force is \(30-20=10\text{ N}\), which is the weight of a volume of water equal to the object's volume. The object weighs three times as much as that water, so it is three times as dense.

questions.stem: Three open containers with different shapes have bases of equal area and are filled with water to the same height. One has vertical sides, one widens toward the top, and one narrows toward the top. How do the forces exerted by the water on the bases of the containers compare?
choices: The force is greatest in the container that widens, because it holds the most water.
The force is greatest in the container that narrows, because the water is compressed.
The force equals the weight of the water in each container, so all three are different.
They are equal, because the pressure at the base depends only on the depth of the water.
questions.explanation: The gauge pressure at depth \(h\) is \(\rho gh\) whatever the shape of the container, and the bases have equal areas, so the forces are equal. In the containers with slanted sides, the walls exert vertical forces on the water that account for the difference between that force and the water's weight.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic lift, the area of the large piston is 20 times the area of the small piston. The fluid is incompressible. How far must the small piston be pushed down to raise a car on the large piston by \(0.10\text{ m}\)?
questions.explanation: The volume of fluid pushed out of the small cylinder equals the volume that enters the large one, so \(A_sd_s=A_Ld_L\) and \(d_s=20(0.10)=2.0\text{ m}\). The force is multiplied by 20, but the work done is the same on both sides.

questions.stem: A diver is \(20\text{ m}\) below the surface of a lake. The density of the water is \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\), atmospheric pressure is \(1.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\), and \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\). What is the absolute pressure at the diver's depth?
questions.explanation: The gauge pressure is \(\rho gh=1000(10)(20)=2.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\). The absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure, for \(3.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\).

questions.stem: A block of wood with density \(500\text{ kg/m}^3\) is held at rest by a string attached to the bottom of a tank of water, with the block completely submerged. The density of water is \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\). The string is cut. Neglecting drag, what is the acceleration of the block immediately afterward?
choices: Zero, because the block was in equilibrium
questions.explanation: The buoyant force is \(\rho_{\text{water}}Vg\), twice the block's weight \(\rho_{\text{wood}}Vg\). The net force is therefore equal to the weight and directed upward, giving an acceleration of \(g\) upward. Before the cut, the string supplied a downward force equal to the block's weight.

questions.stem: Water flows at \(2.0\text{ m/s}\) through a hose of radius \(1.0\text{ cm}\) and leaves through a nozzle of radius \(0.25\text{ cm}\). What is the speed of the water as it leaves the nozzle?
questions.explanation: The volume flow rate \(Av\) is constant. The radius decreases by a factor of 4, so the area decreases by a factor of 16 and the speed increases by a factor of 16, to \(32\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: A block floats in fresh water, as shown. The block is then placed in salt water, which is denser than fresh water. How do the buoyant force on the block and the volume of the block that is submerged compare with their values in fresh water?
choices: The buoyant force is greater and the submerged volume is the same.
The buoyant force is greater and the submerged volume is smaller.
The buoyant force is the same and the submerged volume is smaller.
The buoyant force is the same and the submerged volume is the same.
questions.explanation: A floating block is in equilibrium, so the buoyant force equals the block's weight in either liquid. The buoyant force also equals the weight of the displaced liquid, and a smaller volume of the denser liquid has that weight.

questions.stem: A large open tank is filled with water to height \(H\), as shown. One small hole is made at depth \(h\) below the surface, and a second small hole is made at height \(h\) above the ground. How do the horizontal distances at which the two streams land compare?
choices: The stream from the lower hole lands farther away, because it leaves with a greater speed.
The stream from the upper hole lands farther away, because it falls for a longer time.
The answer depends on whether \(h\) is less than or greater than \(\dfrac{H}{2}\).
questions.explanation: A stream from depth \(d\) leaves with speed \(\sqrt{2gd}\) and falls for a time \(\sqrt{2(H-d)/g}\), so it lands \(2\sqrt{d(H-d)}\) away. Depths of \(h\) and \(H-h\) give the same product: the upper stream is slower but falls longer by exactly the compensating amount.

questions.stem: A solid metal cube hangs from a string and is completely submerged in a tank of water. The cube is lowered until it is twice as deep, still without touching the bottom. Treating water as incompressible, how does the tension in the string change?
choices: It decreases, because the pressure on the cube is greater at the greater depth.
It increases, because more water lies above the cube.
It stays the same, because the buoyant force depends on the volume of water displaced, not on depth.
It decreases, because the buoyant force is proportional to depth.
questions.explanation: The pressures on the top and bottom faces both increase with depth, but their difference, which produces the buoyant force, depends only on the height of the cube. The buoyant force and the cube's weight are unchanged, so the tension is unchanged.

questions.stem: A beaker of water sits on a scale. A student lowers a finger into the water without touching the beaker, and no water spills. What happens to the reading on the scale?
choices: It stays the same, because the finger is supported by the student and does not touch the beaker.
It increases by an amount equal to the buoyant force on the finger.
It increases by an amount equal to the weight of the finger.
It decreases, because the water exerts an upward force on the finger.
questions.explanation: The water exerts an upward buoyant force on the finger, so by Newton's third law the finger exerts an equal downward force on the water, and that force is passed on to the scale. Equivalently, the water level rises, increasing the pressure on the bottom of the beaker.

questions.stem: A block with a volume of \(1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3\) and a density of \(3000\text{ kg/m}^3\) hangs from scale 1 and is completely submerged in water of density \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\), as shown. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what does scale 1 read?
questions.explanation: The block weighs \(3000(1.0\times 10^{-3})(10)=30\text{ N}\). The buoyant force is the weight of the displaced water, \(1000(1.0\times 10^{-3})(10)=10\text{ N}\). The scale supplies the rest: \(30-10=20\text{ N}\).

questions.stem: Before the block shown is lowered into the water, scale 2 reads \(50\text{ N}\). The block weighs \(30\text{ N}\), and the water exerts a buoyant force of \(10\text{ N}\) on it. What does scale 2 read once the block is submerged without touching the beaker?
questions.explanation: The water pushes up on the block with \(10\text{ N}\), so the block pushes down on the water with \(10\text{ N}\), and that force reaches scale 2. The other \(20\text{ N}\) of the block's weight is held by scale 1, not the beaker.

questions.stem: The submerged block shown is lowered slowly to a greater depth, still without touching the beaker. Treating water as incompressible, how do the readings of the two scales change?
questions.explanation: The buoyant force depends on the volume of water displaced, not on depth, so the force on the block and its reaction on the water are unchanged. The pressure on every face rises with depth, but the difference between top and bottom does not.

questions.stem: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows from a cross-sectional area of \(0.020\text{ m}^2\) to \(0.010\text{ m}^2\). The speed in the wide section is \(2.0\text{ m/s}\), and the density of water is \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\). How much greater is the pressure in the wide section than in the narrow section?
questions.explanation: Continuity gives \(4.0\text{ m/s}\) in the narrow section. Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe gives \(\Delta P=\tfrac{1}{2}(1000)\left(4.0^2-2.0^2\right)=6000\text{ Pa}\).

questions.stem: Atmospheric pressure is \(1.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\) and water has a density of \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\). Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), at what depth in a lake is the absolute pressure twice atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: The absolute pressure is \(P_{\text{atm}}+\rho gh\). It doubles when the gauge pressure equals atmospheric pressure: \(1000(10)h=1.0\times 10^5\), so \(h=10\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: A hose with a cross-sectional area of \(2.0\text{ cm}^2\) fills a \(20\text{ L}\) bucket in \(40\text{ s}\). What is the speed of the water in the hose? \((1\text{ L}=1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3)\)
questions.explanation: The flow rate is \(\dfrac{0.020\text{ m}^3}{40\text{ s}}=5.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3\text{/s}\). The area is \(2.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2\), so \(v=\dfrac{Q}{A}=2.5\text{ m/s}\). Converting square centimeters as if they were \(10^{-2}\text{ m}^2\) gives the wrong powers of ten.

questions.stem: A helium balloon is tied to the floor of a closed car and floats upright. The car accelerates forward. Which way does the balloon tilt, and why?
choices: Backward, because objects tend to stay at rest
Backward, because the string pulls it toward the back of the car
It stays upright, because the air moves with the car
Forward, because the accelerating air is at higher pressure toward the back of the car, which pushes the balloon forward
questions.explanation: To accelerate the air forward, the back of the car must push it, so pressure increases from front to back. The less-dense balloon is pushed toward lower pressure, forward, just as it rises against the vertical pressure gradient caused by gravity.

questions.stem: A glass is filled to the brim with water, and an ice cube floats in it. What happens as the ice melts?
choices: The water level stays the same, and no water overflows.
Water overflows, because the ice adds water to the glass.
The water level drops, because ice is less dense than water.
Water overflows, because melting ice expands.
questions.explanation: The floating ice displaces a mass of water equal to its own mass. When it melts, it becomes exactly that mass of water, which fills the volume it had been displacing.

questions.stem: Water flows steadily from a wide pipe into a narrower pipe. How do the volume flow rate and the flow speed in the narrow pipe compare with those in the wide pipe?
choices: The volume flow rate and the speed are both greater.
The volume flow rate is smaller, and the speed is the same.
The volume flow rate is the same, and the speed is greater.
The volume flow rate is smaller, and the speed is greater.
questions.explanation: An incompressible fluid cannot accumulate, so the volume passing each section per second, \(Av\), is the same everywhere. A smaller area therefore requires a larger speed.
